messages.content:
Background – Land Ownership within the Reservation 
My discussion is going to focus on who owns the minerals underlying the Missouri River within the Fort Berthold Reservation. 
To provide a very brief background for land ownership within the reservation:
During the late 1800s – early 1900s under the Federal policy of Allotment 
	– the reservation was split up into individual parcels (40, 80 and 160 acre tracts) and allotted these parcels to individual members;  
These are ‘individual trust lands’  The United States holds title to these lands for the benefit of individuals.  
	Title to these tracts descend to heirs or devisees (By will or intestacy) through BIA probate administration.  Entire presentations could focus on the rules of descent and distribution for allotted interests.  To very briefly touch on this – for those allotted interest owners who died intestate since July 2006 - The Am. Indian Probate Reform Act applies when no approved Tribal probate code is in place.  Before that change in the law, it was the state rules of intestacy where the lands were located.
	– The 3 Affiliated Tribes are also the owners of lands held by the U.S. for the benefit of the Tribes –
	– lands that are not ‘trust’ are Fee – 
Fee lands can be owned by non-Indians, Indians or the Tribes.  At one time they may have been trust, but have passed out of that restricted status.  They may also have never been allotted and be returned to trust status through the BIA processes.
Allotment policy was abandoned in the 1920s and it is generally acknowledged as a failure.  It has created several ownership issues as it relates to individual allotments because a 160-acre parcel may be owned by upwards to several hundred people (through probate determinations made by the BIA since the early 1900s). It has also resulted in a checkerboard of ownership 160-acre trust, then a fee tract, then a tribal tract, etc… 
Title documents for the Fort Berthold Reservation are maintained at the BIA Regional Offices in Aberdeen, SD – Land Titles and Records Office.  You have to have permission to view the records (usually can only be granted by a company or person who owns an interest affected by the records you’re asking to review).  The Aberdeen Regional Office provides services to the Great Plains Region Tribes defined as those located in North and South Dakota & Nebraska.
There are several great resources to learn more about some of the general themes in Federal Indian Law – Cohen’s Handbook of Federal Indian Law is acknowledged as an encyclopedia of Federal Indian Law and is a great starting point to learn more about a wide range of federal Indian law concepts.  There are also many resources to learn more about the history of the Fort Berthold Reservation. 
Throughout the presentation I will likely refer to the Three Affiliated Tribes as either ‘Tribes’ or the MHA Nation.  
I will be mainly focused on Tribes Trust mineral interests (oil and gas)  which are riparian to the Missouri River and then also discuss the ownership of the minerals underlying the River as the same flows through the boundaries of the reservation.

Map of Boundaries as of 1910 & the approx.. size/location of the River
Here’s a map Courtesy of the ND Studies Program at the State Historical Society of North Dakota. Represents the boundaries as of 1910.  The map also provides the approximate location of the Missouri River in relation to Reservation Communities.
The original description of the Tribes territory in 1851 included approximately 12 million acres and stretched into South Dakota, Montana & Wyoming.  
Through later executive orders and statutes (including Allotment and Homestead) between 1870s and 1910 the size of the reservation was reduced dramatically. 
Originally existed only South of the Missouri River, but as tracts south of the river shrank, the reservation was expanded to the north & east.  The acreage where the reservation was extended do not compare at all to the acreage that was whittled away during those 40 years.
Today the reservation occupies less than 1 million acres in Mercer, Mountrail, McKenzie, Dunn and McLean Counties. However, not all of the tracts within reservation boundaries are owned in trust.
	 – there are vast tracts which are held in fee, free of the restrictions on alienation imposed on trust interests.  
	- Also, it is important to note that tracts which are fee surface may be mineral trust & vice versa.  My focus and the maps for the rest of the presentation will include Mineral Trust tracts. 

Federal Taking – Public Law 81-437
To acquire the FEE lands necessary for the Garrison Dam Project outside of Trust lands within the Fort Berthold Reservation, the Army Corps of Engineers used 1 of 2 methods:  
1) they either obtained deeds from the owners (may or may not have contained a reservation of mineral interests) or 
2) the Corps initiated a private condemnation suit

However, for lands within the Fort Berthold Reservation which the U.S. owned in trust for the Tribes or in trust for the benefit of individuals, the lands needed for the Garrison Dam were taken by federal law.  Public Law 81-437 an Act  “To vest title to certain lands of the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation, North Dakota, in the United States, and to provide compensation therefor.”
The Act describes the exterior boundaries of the takings area – totaling 174,000 acres.  Of that the Act identified 20,000 acres that were not included likely because the tracts were already owned outside of trust status.
The act also describes the relocation of communities & the compensation that had been calculated for all of the taken lands.  
According to 1 report prepared by the Regional Agency Official in 1948 – there were 357 occupied homes on the Reservation in 1948.  
289 homes had to be relocated.  Approx. 80% of families lived within the takings area.  
How the Garrison Dam affected the Tribes is an extremely complex topic.  If anyone is looking for a list of resources to learn more I would be happy to provide it.
ND Studies.org – joint effort by ND Historical Society, Prairie Public & ND Humanities Council
MHANation.com – 
Fort Berthold Community College Library website also provides a great timeline and history of the Tribes

Map AFTER Garrison Dam flooded the area
Here’s another map from the State Historical Society ND Studies Program.  
When you read more about the history of the flooding, an element that comes up quite often is how the reservation was segmented after the flooding.  The map here is a great representation of that.  Areas now completely cut off from one another by the Missouri or by the Little Missouri.
There are several excellent resources for discussion of how the lands within the Fort Berthold Reservation were taken.
Dammed Indians provides a broad look at the effect of the Pick-Sloan Plan on several Tribes along the Missouri River including the Three Affiliated Tribes
The MHA website also provides a history of the Reservation and the website for the Fort Berthold Community College Library also provided some great background information
http://www.mhanation.com/
http://lib.fortbertholdcc.edu/FortBerthold/default.asp

Fort Berthold Reservation Mineral Restoration Act – Public Law 98-602
In 1984, Congress passed the Fort Berthold Reservation Mineral Restoration Act.
“Restoration” is a bit misleading.  The tracts conveyed to the U.S. in trust for the Three Affiliated Tribes were those lands within reservation boundaries that may have been owned in trust for individuals prior to the 1949 takings act OR owned in trust for the Tribes (or even owned in fee where the private conveyance to the U.S. or the condemnation action did not provide for a reservation of mineral interests to the prior owners).
So, while they refer to it as ‘restoration’ act and in some respects it is, it is also a conveyance of interests to the U.S. in trust for the Tribes.
Before the act was passed the mineral interests were being leased pursuant to BLM policies (at least as late as 1982).  You can find references to these now expired Federal Leases by searching the BLM Serial Register Pages.
The Restoration Act requires that development of the mineral interests is subject to regulations which may be imposed by the Sec. of the Army (Army Corps)

Trust Minerals zoomed out – Tribal & Individual Trust interests
Green outlined tracts represents minerals of which are partially or entirely owned by the U.S. in trust for the Tribes or by the U.S. for the benefit of Individuals. 
Also – the green oil derricks are representations of the actual drilling rigs that are operating within the reservation. 
The GIS Map Server available through the ND Industrial Commission – Department of Mineral Resources, Oil & Gas Division website allows you to select various layers of information.  This green layer is the Fort Berthold Mineral Tracts. 
-	It is difficult to tell from this zoomed out perspective, but there are numerous tracts which are not outlined in green which have passed out of trust status. – Either never allotted or tracts that were once owned in trust but for which fee patents have since been issued (tracts have been inherited by non-Indians or app. by Indians for Fee patents) 
-	Later maps will be zoomed in to provide a better sense of oil and gas development near and under the river

Fractionation & Public Law 105-188
Before we get too involved in the riverbed within reservation boundaries.  
I thought I’d take a little detour to tell you a little bit about another federal law impacting the leasing of individual allotted mineral interests within the Fort Berthold Reservation
 – The original Mineral Leasing Act requires 100% consent of individual allottees for the BIA to issue a lease (with the thought that there was only 1 owner or perhaps 1 family that owned an undivided tract – 40 acres, 80 acres, etc…) 
	***Issue off fractionation*** few tracts are owned by a single person Example indicates what happens through generations.  
-	In my scenario Imagine the Original Allottee owned 100% which passed to her 3 kids; I’ve left it off, but it would take 2 of the 3 kids to consent to the lease .  
-	Then -  2 of the 3 kids have multiple children of their own – now you’re looking at 1/9 and 1/12 interests.  
-	In the 3rd Generation – you have split 1/12 into 3 - 1/36 pieces and by the 4th generation that 1/36 interest is split into 1/144 (approx. 0.694% interest) that you cannot even read on this page.  In an 80 acre tract a 1/144 interest is the equivalent of 0.556 acres.
In response to the problem of obtaining 100% consent to develop lands, Congress passed Public Law 108-188 ---- the Fort Berthold Mineral Leasing Act passed July 7, 1998
-	Provides that the BIA can approve leases once owners representing a majority of the mineral interests have consented to the lease
As indicated by the total acceptance at the bottom the goal is to achieve acceptance by the majority of the interests not the majority of the owners
-	This was originally ONLY for Fort Berthold +++ As the success of ‘majority consent to lease’ was recognized it has been extended to other reservations.

Along the River – zoomed in from original
In this map we’ve zoomed in a bit more – 
The black lines on this map represent the horizontal legs of wells.  As you can tell on this map, there is a great deal of activity occurring on sections that include portions of the river.
According to the ND Department of Trust Lands there are 31 wells currently producing oil and/or gas from spacing units which include portions of the Missouri River within the reservation boundaries.

Same Approx. view – new layer
Here is the same approximate view, but without the blue map overlay approximating the current Missouri River.  The sliver between the green on both sides represents the approx. location of the Missouri River when the original GLO Survey was completed/at the original time of allotment of lands within the reservation.
This does not represent where the river was in 1953 and does not reflect where water currently flows across these tracts.
Between the original GLO survey & the approximation of the River as available through the oil and gas division’s website, the river has changed dramatically

Questions Presented – 
With all of that background information in mind:  
Who owns the Missouri River within the Fort Berthold Reservation?  
-	State or The Tribes?
-	If the State owns the riverbed, the Tribes and the State will have to resolve the issue of location/acreage
-	If the Tribes own the riverbed, the U.S. in trust for the Tribes and the Tribes will have to determine the issue of location/acreage
-	Various ownership theories for the Tribes suggest that the Tribe is the owner of the bed of the Missouri River within the Fort Berthold Reservation boundaries free of Trust restrictions
-	Thus, if the Tribes win the Riverbed argument & it is determined to be free of trust restrictions – By the Restoration act, the U.S. in trust for the Tribes acquire vast tracts of minerals riparian to the river; 
Where is the River? – is it the bed of the Missouri River prior to the flooding of the lands as a result of the Garrison Dam? Is it the Present “River” also referred to as Lake Sakakawea?
-	Matters for the State discussion & for the Tribes discussion
-	Arguably, either the State or the Tribes could claim the entire ‘Lake’ is riverbed.
-	The 1953 ish mark of the river (at or near the time the lands were flooded) is the other option.
What line do you use to calculate acreage?
-	BEST information about the course of the Missouri River at the time of the taking of the lands for the Garrison Dam and at the time just prior to the lands being flooded after the Dam was closed are aerial photographs.  These photographs can be used to calculate acreage.  In fact, that appears to be the method the State has used to calculate acreage for leasing.  
-	I can only imagine the various interpretations that surveying professionals will come up with in interpreting the ordinary high & ordinary low based on black and white aerial photographs.

Another view – another set of layers
-	The image on the left indicates the approximate river (bright blue) with the Trust mineral tracts
-	On the right – approx. same view with a satellite image overlay
At this zoomed in state on the left you can begin to see the shading difference between Tribal Trust Mineral Tracts and Individual Trust mineral tracts – the Tribal tracts are just a bit darker and can be seen mainly along the river in the image on the left.  These tracts along and in some cases submerged are owned in Trust for the Tribes pursuant to the Mineral Restoration Act.

Possible Considerations – looking at SOME cases – 
Now – we’ll talk about federal cases as the same relate to Tribal or Federal claims to water bodies with the effect of defeating State Title to said water body
Before I start going into any details:
The case law establishes a strong presumption that the United States retained title to the bed of navigable waters for the benefit of future states & upon the state’s admission to the Union, the State acquired the riverbed subject to the U.S. navigability easement for commerce
Also – some of the cases or the dissenting opinions – discuss what is often referred to as the Indian Canon of Construction.  To put it very simply, ambiguities in treaties are to be resolved in favor of a Tribe as that Tribe would have understood the term
As of August 2012, there are 566 federally recognized tribes in the 48 contiguous states plus Alaska ---- It is important to note that every tribe has a unique history - Historic and cultural development, and the relationship & interactions with the federal government.  
In several instances, the cases involving a Tribe’s claim to river have focused on that Tribe’s unique characteristics or History in determining whether the Tribe was the owner of the bed of a river.  The general considerations that are discussed in these cases may or may not be an important factor in determining ownership of the minerals underlying the Missouri River within the Fort Berthold Reservation.  However, they do present a broad overview of what has been considered in the past.
It is also important to consider that the Supreme Court cases were split decisions - sometimes based on a plurality.  Indicating that these are not easy decisions to make.  Strong arguments exist for both sides.  
One factor that was relevant to ownership of a navigable river is the History of a reservation boundaries
-	Idaho v. United States – the United States brought suit to quiet title to a portion of Lake Coeur d’Alene in Northern Idaho in the Coeur d’Alene Tribe.  The earliest description of the reservation did not include the lake, but the Tribes petitioned the Federal Government and in 1873 the reservation was described to include nearly all of the lake and a portion of the St. Joe River (navigable according to the Coast Guard).  However, the treaties describing the reservation in 1873 were not ratified.
-	By 1889, the United States had negotiated with the Coeur d’Alene Tribe for the Northern portion of the reservation including 2/3 of the Lake – The Court points out that while the treaties identifying the reservation had not been ratified, the only party negotiated with for these northern lands was the Coeur d’Alene Tribe
-	Another defining consideration in this case was the description of the Lake – the normal practice of using meander lines to describe boundaries around water bodies was not used in the description of the Coeur d’Alene reservation.  Rather it was a straight line across the lake.  
-	Ultimately, the U.S. in trust for the Tribe is determined to own the 1/3 of Lake Coeur d’Alene & the portion of the St. Joe River within the reservation boundaries.
Next – whether the water body in question was an important part of the Tribe’s way of life
-	Montana v. United States – Here, the Crow Tribe attempted to regulate hunting and fishing by non-Indians on lands which were owned in fee by non-members within the boundaries of the reservation – part of its jurisdictional claim rested on owning the Big Horn River as it flowed through the reservation
-	The Court determined that the Crow Tribe DID NOT obtain the bed of the River when the reservation was established because the treaties of 1851 & 1868 did not contain sufficient language to overcome the strong presumption that the U.S. retained title to riverbed for ultimate conveyance to the future State: Specifically, the treaties 1) did not describe the river & 2) the river was not important to the Crow Tribe’s way of life (implying that ownership of the river was therefore not essential)
-	NOTE:  Montana v. United States is most often cited in federal Indian law for its jurisdictional precedent but discussion of the case in terms of what it stands for in the jurisdictional analysis is not relevant to the questions presented
Another element that has been discussed in cases – the length of time the Tribe has occupied the area 
In Yankton Sioux Tribe v. South Dakota the District Court had found that Lake Andes (Navigable lake) was navigable and that the Yankton Sioux Tribe owned the lakebed under treaty entered in 1858
-	The 8th Circuit rejected the claim that the Yankton Sioux Tribe owned Lake Andes under Aboriginal Title because the Tribe could not establish title to the time before the Louisiana Purchase (when the U.S. obtained title to the lands).  So the Louisiana Purchase pre-dated the Aboriginal Title claim and thus defeated the aboriginal title claim.
-	The Court pointed out that the Yankton Sioux Tribe could prove their exclusive occupancy of the lands surrounding Lake Andes as of 1810, but not before the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.
-	The Tribe here did not attempt to argue that the U.S. had divested itself of the lakebed per the 1858 treaty – to put it another way, the Tribe did not claim to have title because of a grant from the U.S. (thus no argument that the U.S. intended to defeat the future state’s title was made)

Additional Cases
United States v. Alaska – Court determines that submerged lands near National Petroleum Reserve are part of National Petroleum Reserve & therefore owned by the United States
-	Only Congress has the power to convey title to U.S. lands (per Article IV, Section 3, clause 2 of the Constitution)
-	Executive Order of 1923 used as 1 premise for why submerged lands bordering the National Petroleum Reserve were NOT included in the navigable waters obtained by Alaska at Statehood
-	This involved a reservation of federal title to the submerged lands (not a conveyance to a 3rd party)
-	Other defining characteristic – involved Coastal lands
-	Emphasized the ‘purpose’ element in determining that Alaska’s ownership of submerged coastal lands defeats the purpose of setting aside the Petroleum Reserve – for satisfy future military needs.  Here, the Court determined that the U.S. owned the submerged lands adjacent to the Reserve because that ownership was necessary to prevent the draining of the Reserve’s petroleum Resources
Utah Division of State Lands v. United States - 
Pre-statehood Reservation – The Sundry Appropriations Act of 1888 called on officials to select sites for reservoirs or other hydraulic works for irrigation or flood protection purposes – An offficial selected Utah Lake as such a site - The 1888 act was repealed in 1890, but the repeal provided that the lands already selected would still be reserved & no future settlement would be allowed
- The Court doesn’t answer the question of whether a Federal “Reservation” is sufficient to defeat state title because here the purpose of reserving the site (Reservoir for irrigiation or flood purposes) not frustrated by State acquiring title – Here the Court determined that Utah was the owner of the bed of Utah Lake

One last map – 
As a last visual – I’ll leave you with another shot of rig locations and a zoomed out area of the river 
Both the ND Department of Trust Lands and the Three Affiliated Tribes are leasing mineral interests underlying the bed of the Missouri River.
Leasing by the State appears to be limited to the location of the river near the time of the flooding of the tracts.
31 wells have been spud and are producing on spacing units that include portions of the Missouri River
As of March 7 – no negotiations between the ND Dept of Trust Lands and the Three Affiliated Tribes  & no litigation to resolve the dispute has been initiated.
For State leases issued since some rule changes went into effect in 2010, companies developing mineral interests from ‘disputed ownership areas’ must hold the royalties in escrow accounts at the Bank of North Dakota.  However, for areas producing under state leases issued before 2010 (affected by the Riverbed dispute), the companies are not required to report to the state. So there is no estimate of the royalties which are accruing to the ‘disputed areas.’
Based on the maps available through the NDIC Dept of Mineral Resources, companies are continuing to develop spacing units that include riverbed tracts.  
It could be years before all of the questions that we’ve presented to you are answered by the State Supreme Court and possibly even the U.S. Supreme Court.
 

Thank you for your attention
Recognizing that we are the last speakers on the agenda.  2 things to finish up with, we’d be happy to answer any of your questions if you want to come up and visit with us.  Also, if anyone is interesting in receiving a bound copy of the presentation materials, come up with your card and we can mail you on in the next few weeks.   


 	
	
	
RE:	Pipeline Rights of Way - First Steps


I have been asked to prepare an explanation of the process to obtain rights of way for the construction of oil and gas pipelines across lands lying within the boundaries of the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation which are held by the United States of America for the benefit of the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation or for the benefit of individual Indians.

The general source of authority for the granting of rights of way across Indian Lands is found in Title 25 of the United States Code, Chapter 8, with regulations implementing the general authority found in 25 C.F.R. Part 169.

25 U.S.C. §321 – Rights-of-way for pipelines

Section 321 of Title 25 of the United States Code specifically authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to grant rights-of-way for the “construction, operation, and maintenance of pipe lines for the conveyance of oil and gas through any Indian reservation,” through lands held by the United States of America in trust for an Indian Tribe or any individual Indian or lands reserved for an Indian Agency, Indian school or reserved for other purpose in connection with the Indian Service (hereinafter, “Indian Lands”). 25 U.S.C. § 321

Rights-of-way granted under 25 U.S.C. §321 are limited in duration to 20 years.  25 C.F.R. § 169.25 (b).  Renewals of these rights-of-way may be requested through the procedure described in 25 C.F.R. § 169.19.

Rights-of-way for lateral lines sought under 25 U.S.C. § 321 may not require approval by the Secretary of the Interior where all of the affected individual owners have consented.  However,  the provisions of 25 C.F.R. Part 169 require consent of both the land owners and consent of the Secretary of the Interior for all rights-of-way. See 25 C.F.R. § 169.3 (a) and (b).  Thus, regardless of the provisions of 25 U.S.C. § 321 to the contrary, consent of the Secretary of the Interior is required for all pipeline rights-of-way across Indian Lands. 

25 U.S.C. § 323 -  Rights-of-way for all purposes across any Indian lands

Section 323 of Title 25 of the United States Code authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to grant rights-of-way, “for all purposes, subject to such conditions as he may prescribe, over and across any lands now or hereafter held in trust by the United States for individual Indians or Indian tribes…, or any lands now or hereafter owned, subject to restrictions against alienation by individual Indians or Indian tribes…, and any other lands heretofore or hereafter acquired or set aside for the use and benefit of the Indians.” 25 U.S.C. §323.  Authority to establish the regulations for the implementation of 25 U.S.C. § 323 are specifically delegated to the Secretary of the Interior in 25 U.S.C. § 328.

According to 25 C.F.R. § 169.18, rights-of-way granted under the Act of February 5, 1948 (62 Stat. 17; 25 U.S.C. §§ 323-328), for the specific purposes outlined in said section, including oil and gas pipelines, may be granted without limitation as to term of years.  Rights-of-way granted for other purposes, “shall be for a period of not to exceed 50 years, as determined by the Secretary and stated in the conveyance instrument.” 25 C.F.R. § 169.18.  However, 25 C.F.R. § 169.25 regarding oil and gas pipelines, specifically, limit the duration of rights-of-way for oil and gas pipelines to a 20 year period which may be extended by applying for renewal of rights-of-way grants as described in 25 C.F.R. § 169.19.

Permission to Survey

With the two statutes authorizing the Secretary of the Interior to grant rights-of-way across Indian lands for the purpose of constructing and maintaining an oil or gas pipeline in mind, we now turn to the steps which must be taken to apply for such a right-of-way.

Prior to the submission of any application for a right-of-way, the Secretary of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, must first authorize the applicant to conduct a survey of the lands the proposed pipeline will cross.  The written application for permission to survey must include:

1.	Adequate description of the proposed project, including the purpose and general location

2.	Consents to survey executed by a majority of the owners of the lands to be surveyed not including any fee ownership in said lands.

Note:	Information regarding ownership of lands lying within the Fort Berthold Reservation can be obtained by contacting the Fort Berthold Agency office and requesting uncertified Title Status Reports and Address Reports for all allotted and tribally owned tracts for which permission to survey is being requested.

3.	Evidence of good faith and financial responsibility of the applicant

4.	Check or money order sufficient to cover twice the estimated damages which may be sustained as a result of the survey.  A surety bond may be substituted in lieu of check or money order with approval of the Secretary so long as the company issuing such a surety bond is licensed to do business in the state where the land to be surveyed is located, in this case North Dakota.

5.	Agreement to indemnify  the United States, the owners of the land, and occupants of the land, against liability for loss of life, personal injury and property damage occurring because of survey activities and caused by the applicant, his employees, contractors and their employees, or subcontractors and their employees.

6.	The following additional information must be included in the application if:

	a.	Applicant is a Corporation: a copy of the corporation’s charter or articles of incorporation certified by the proper state official of the state where the corporation was organized and a copy of the resolution or bylaws of the corporation authorizing the filing of the application. “When the land covered by the application is located in a State other than that in which the application was incorporated, it must also submit a certificate of the proper State official that the applicant is authorized to do business in the State where the land is located.”

	b.	Applicant is an unincorporated Partnership or Association: certified copies of the articles of partnership or association, or if none, the signature of each member of the partnership or association accompanied by a statement that no articles of partnership or association exist.

Upon receipt of the above described application for Permission to Survey, the Secretary may grant the applicant written permission to survey.

Survey the proposed pipeline locations

In speaking with Emily Dawes of the Fort Berthold Agency Office in New Town, after permission to survey has been granted, the applicant should coordinate said survey with the Tribal Historic Preservation Office and the Fort Berthold Agency Environmental Office along with the firm hired to conduct the survey to schedule completion of the survey.  Additional information regarding scheduling the survey is included in the grant of permission to survey.

Application for Right-of-Way

Applications for rights of way should be filed in duplicate with the Secretary of the Interior.  The application should include the following: 

1.	The statute under which the right-of-way is sought

2.	Specific use requested

3.	Width and length of desired right-of-way

4.	Evidence of good faith and financial responsibility of the applicant

5.	The following additional information must be included in the application if:

	a.	Applicant is a Corporation: a copy of the corporation’s charter or articles of incorporation certified by the proper state official of the state where the corporation was organized and a copy of the resolution or bylaws of the corporation authorizing the filing of the application. “When the land covered by the application is located in a State other than that in which the application was incorporated, it must also submit a certificate of the proper State official that the applicant is authorized to do business in the State where the land is located.”

	b.	Applicant is an unincorporated Partnership or Association: certified copies of the articles of partnership or association, or if none, the signature of each member of the partnership or association accompanied by a statement that no articles of partnership or association exist.

6.	Stipulation, executed in duplicate, expressly agreeing to the following:

“(a) To construct and maintain the right-of-way in a workmanlike manner.

(b) To pay promptly all damages and compensation, in addition to the deposit made pursuant to §169.4, determined by the Secretary to be due the landowners and authorized users and occupants of the land on account of the survey, granting, construction and maintenance of the right-of-way.

(c) To indemnify the landowners and authorized users and occupants against any liability for loss of life, personal injury and property damage arising from the construction, maintenance, occupancy or use of the lands by the applicant, his employees, contractors and their employees, or subcontractors and their employees.

(d) To restore the lands as nearly as may be possible to their original condition upon the completion of construction to the extent compatible with the purpose for which the right-of-way was granted.

(e) To clear and keep clear the lands within the right-of-way to the extent compatible with the purpose of the right-of-way; and to dispose of all vegetative and other material cut, uprooted, or otherwise accumulated during the construction and maintenance of the project.

(f) To take soil and resource conservation and protection measures, including weed control, on the land covered by the right-of-way.

(g) To do everything reasonably within its power to prevent and suppress fires on or near the lands to be occupied under the right-of-way.

(h) To build and repair such roads, fences, and trails as may be destroyed or injured by construction work and to build and maintain necessary and suitable crossings for all roads and trails that intersect the works constructed, maintained, or operated under the right-of-way.

(i) That upon revocation or termination of the right-of-way, the applicant shall, so far as is reasonably possible, restore the land to its original condition.

(j) To at all times keep the Secretary informed of its address, and in case of corporations, of the address of its principal place of business and of the names and addresses of its principal officers.

(k) That the applicant will not interfere with the use of the lands by or under the authority of the landowners for any purpose not inconsistent with the primary purpose for which the right-of-way is granted.” 25 C.F.R. § 169.5 (a)-(k).

7.	Maps of definite location as more fully described in 25 C.F.R. § 169.6, with sufficient references to the field notes, “so as to make it convenient to follow field notes.” 25 C.F.R. § 169.6.

8.	Field Notes which were prepared as a result of the survey conducted across the proposed right-of-way route as more fully described in 25 C.F.R. § 169.7.

9.	Affidavit of the Engineer who made the survey, “certifying to the accuracy of the survey and maps and designating by termini and length in miles and decimals, the line of route for which the right-of-way application is made” 25 C.F.R. § 169.9.

10.	Affidavit of the applicant, “certifying to the accuracy of the survey and maps and designating by termini and length in miles and decimals, the line of route for which the right-of-way application is made” 25 C.F.R. § 169.9.

11.	Consents to Right-of-Way executed by individual owners and the Three Affiliated Tribes representing a majority of the interest owners in each tract the proposed pipeline will cross. 25 C.F.R. § 169.3 (a) and (b).

12.	Size of the proposed pipeline and whether the pipe is welded, screw-joint, dresser, or other type of coupling

13.	If applicant seeks rights-of-way for pumping stations or for tank-site purposes, these additional uses should be clearly identified on the maps and must be accompanied by a stipulation agreeing to the following provisions as described in 25 C.F.R. § 169.25 (e) (1) and (2):

(a) Upon abandonment of the right-of-way to level all dikes, fire-guards, and excavations and to remove all concrete masonry foundations, bases, and structural works and to restore the land as nearly as may be possible to its original condition.

(b) That a grant for pumping station or tank site purposes shall be subservient to the owner's right to remove or authorize the removal of oil, gas, or other mineral deposits; and that the structures for pumping station or tank site will be removed or relocated if necessary to avoid interference with the exploration for or recovery of oil, gas, or other minerals.

In addition to each of the above requirements for submitting an application for right-of-way, at the time of filing the application:

[T]he applicant must deposit with the Secretary the total estimated consideration and damages, which shall include consideration for the right-of-way, severance damages, damages caused during the survey, and estimated damages to result from construction less any deposit previously made under [25 C.F.R.] §169.4. In no case shall the amount deposited as consideration for the right-of-way over any parcel be less than the amount specified in the consent covering that parcel. If in reviewing the application, the Secretary determines that the amounts deposited are inadequate to compensate the owners, the applicant shall increase the deposit to an amount determined by the Secretary to be adequate. The amounts so deposited shall be held in a “special deposit” account for distribution to or for the account of the landowners and authorized users and occupants of the land. Amounts deposited to cover damages resulting from survey and construction may be disbursed after the damages have been sustained. Amounts deposited to cover consideration for the right-of-way and severance damages shall be disbursed upon the granting of the right-of-way. Any part of the deposit which is not required for disbursement as aforesaid shall be refunded to the applicant promptly following receipt of the affidavit of completion of construction filed pursuant to [25 C.F.R.] §169.16.  25 C.F.R. § 169.14

Action on the Application 

According to 25 C.F.R. § 169.15, following the completion of each of the above application requirements, the Secretary of the Interior is authorized to grant the right-of-way by issuance of a conveyance instrument in the form approved by the Secretary.  This instrument shall incorporate all restrictions and conditions which were set forth in the consents to right-of-way executed by the owners of the relevant tracts.  The Maps of definite location may be attached and incorporated into the conveyance instrument by reference.  The Secretary of the Interior, may authorize a single right-of-way covering all tracts in an application or may grant rights-of-way covering one or more tracts included in the application.  The right-of-way conveyance instrument is then filed in the appropriate office of record for land documents, in this case, the appropriate office is likely the Great Plains Regional Land Titles and Records Office, Aberdeen, South Dakota.

Affidavit of Completion

When construction of any right-of-way is complete, the applicant should file an affidavit of completion, executed by the engineer and certified by the applicant. 25 C.F.R. § 169.16.  A copy of this affidavit is then transmitted to the appropriate office of record for land documents. Failure to file said affidavit is grounds for cancellation of the right-of-way in accordance with 25 C.F.R. § 169.20.

Conclusion

Any individual or entity seeking a right-of-way across Indian lands, as defined above, should first submit an application for permission to survey which must include consents to survey executed by a majority of the interest owners in each relevant tract.  Following the grant of permission to survey, the Tribal Historical Preservation Office and the Bureau of Indian Affairs Environmental office will be consulted to complete the survey.  Subsequently, the application with all accompanying information described above should be submitted to the Bureau of Indian Affairs for approval.  The application for right-of-way must also include consents to right-of-way executed by a majority of the interest owners in each relevant tract.

10/2/1984--Passed Senate amended.    (There is 1 other summary) 
(Measure passed Senate, amended) 
Title I: Wyandotte Tribe of Oklahoma - Directs the Wyandotte Tribe of Oklahoma and the Secretary of the Interior to update tribal membership rolls according to prescribed guidelines for the purpose of distributing specified judgment funds to such Tribe. 
Requires the Secretary to publish notice in the appropriate media regarding the per capita distribution of the judgment funds and the application procedures for the distribution. 
Requires the Secretary to allocate the judgment funds between the Wyandotte Tribe of Oklahoma and the Absentee Wyandottes according to prescribed guidelines. 
Requires that the Wyandotte Tribe allocation be divided: (1) 80 percent for per capita distribution; and (2) 20 percent for specified uses for the benefit of the Tribe. 
States that such 20 percent allocation may be distributed by the Wyandotte Tribe without seeking the Secretary's approval. Exempts the Secretary from further trust responsibility regarding the 20 percent allocation. 
Exempts the judgment funds distribution from: (1) Federal, State or local income taxes; or (2) any consideration as a resource for purposes of public assistance eligibility criteria. 
Repeals specified law regarding the use and distribution of specified judgment funds. 
Title II: Fort Berthold Reservation Mineral Restoration Act - Fort Berthold Reservation Mineral Restoration Act - Declares that mineral rights in specified lands are held in trust by the United States for the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation. 
Requires any exploration or development regarding such mineral rights to comply with regulations prescribed by the Secretary of the Army. 
Authorizes the United States to renew or extend leases or contracts concerning such mineral interests under certain conditions. 
Declares that revenues from such mineral interests which accrue to the United States after enactment of this Act are held in trust for the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation. 
Authorizes the Secretary of the Army and the Secretary of the Interior to enter into agreements to transfer to the United States specified lands held in trust for the Three Affiliated Tribes or any individual Indian. Conditions such transfer upon approval by the affected beneficiaries. Authorizes both Secretaries to enter into agreements to hold certain lands no longer needed for the Garrison Dam and Reservoir Project in trust for the Three Affiliated Tribes. 
Directs the Three Affiliated Tribes to reimburse the United States a fixed sum of $300,000 if net proceeds from mineral interest development exceed $300,000.

### Three Framing Choices Rejected or Reframed by a Tribal Regulator

A Tribal regulator would explicitly reject the neutral, company-centric framing of the original presentation and reframe it to assert Tribal sovereignty, using the provided legal precedents.

1.  **Framing Choice #1: The Missouri Riverbed as an Open Question**
    *   **Original Framing:** Presented the ownership of the riverbed as a debatable issue ("Questions Presented – Who owns the Missouri River? - State or The Tribes?"). It suggested "Strong arguments exist for both sides" and noted that both the State and Tribes are currently leasing tracts.
    *   **Tribal Regulator's Reframe:** The riverbed is unequivocally owned by the Tribes.
    *   **Justification from Text:** The regulator would invoke the **Indian Canon of Construction**, which the original text states resolves ambiguities in treaties "in favor of a Tribe as that Tribe would have understood the term." They would argue the federal government's treatment of the Tribes' territory implies ownership of navigable waters. They would cite ***Idaho v. United States***, where the court looked at the unique history and intent (the non-ratified treaty, the straight-line boundary description) to award ownership of a lakebed to a tribe. They would also point to the **Fort Berthold Reservation Mineral Restoration Act**, arguing that by restoring mineral interests "riparian to the river," the Act presumes the Tribes' underlying ownership of the riverbed itself.

2.  **Framing Choice #2: The Garrison Dam Taking as a Simple Federal Acquisition**
    *   **Original Framing:** Described the taking under Public Law 81-437 as a factual event where the Army Corps acquired land, using deeds or condemnation, and compensated the owners. It mentions the tragic human cost (289 homes relocated) but frames it as a historical event.
    *   **Tribal Regulator's Reframe:** The taking was an illegal seizure of Tribal lands and resources without just compensation, a breach of the federal trust responsibility.
    *   **Justification from Text:** The regulator would highlight that the Act took "lands of the Three Affiliated Tribes... in trust for the Tribes or in trust for the benefit of individuals." They would point out the original text's own admission that the term "Restoration" in the subsequent Mineral Restoration Act is "a bit misleading," implying the lands and minerals were taken in the first place. The regulator would argue that the minimal compensation cited (and the fact that 20,000 acres were excluded as they were not trust lands) underscores the injustice. The Restoration Act is framed as a necessary correction of this historical wrong.

3.  **Framing Choice #3: The Mineral Restoration Act as Merely a "Conveyance"**
    *   **Original Framing:** Called the Act "Restoration" but immediately clarified it was "also a conveyance of interests to the U.S. in trust for the Tribes." It framed the Act's purpose as fixing a leasing issue (moving from BLM to BIA policies).
    *   **Tribal Regulator's Reframe:** The Act was primarily an act of restitution, restoring mineral rights that were unlawfully taken by the Garrison Dam project.
    *   **Justification from Text:** The regulator would emphasize that the Act restored minerals from lands that "may have been owned in trust for individuals prior to the 1949 takings act OR owned in trust for the Tribes." This directly links the Act to the previous taking. The Act's declaration that revenues "accruing to the United States after enactment of this Act are held in trust for the Three Affiliated Tribes" reinforces the idea of restoration of a beneficial interest. The requirement for development to comply with Army Corps regulations is a condition placed on this restored property, not a feature of a simple conveyance.

**INTERNAL MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Energy Company Legal & Operations Team
**FROM:** Legal Compliance Officer
**DATE:** October 26, 2023
**SUBJECT:** Review of Tribal Presentation: Operational Inaccuracies and Legal Gaps Regarding Pipeline ROW Applications

Team,

I have reviewed the newly drafted presentation from the perspective of a Three Affiliated Tribes (TAT) energy regulator. While the presentation provides valuable context on tribal history and sovereignty, it contains several claims and omissions that are operationally inaccurate and legally incomplete when measured against our required pipeline application process, as detailed in Document 2, "Pipeline Rights of Way - First Steps."

Relying on the Tribal presentation alone would expose the company to significant compliance risks. Our procedures are governed by rigid BIA mandates under 25 C.F.R. Part 169, not the simplified, sovereignty-focused narrative presented by the Tribe.

Below are the specific issues I have flagged:

**1. Incomplete and Misleading Description of Consent Requirements.**
The Tribal presentation claims that pipeline construction requires "the necessity of Tribal consent alongside BIA and individual landowner consent." This is dangerously incomplete.

*   **Operational Inaccuracy:** The presentation omits the most critical consent requirement: **the express consent of the Secretary of the Interior is required for all pipeline rights-of-way across Indian Lands.** Document 2 explicitly states, "regardless of the provisions of 25 U.S.C. § 321 to the contrary, consent of the Secretary of the Interior is required for all pipeline rights-of-way across Indian Lands." Our process cannot proceed without this federal approval, which is a non-negotiable step beyond tribal consent.

**2. Omission of the Prerequisite "Permission to Survey" Process.**
The Tribal presentation incorrectly implies that a company can proceed directly to a right-of-way application.

*   **Legally Incomplete:** Document 2 mandates that we must first obtain written permission to survey. This is a separate application process requiring:
    *   Adequate project description.
    *   Consents to survey from a majority of owners.
    *   Evidence of good faith and financial responsibility.
    *   A deposit or surety bond for estimated damages.
    *   An indemnification agreement.
    *   Corporate/partnership documentation.
    *   Only after this permission is granted can we proceed. The Tribal presentation makes no mention of this critical first step.

**3. Grossly Simplified Right-of-Way Application Requirements.**
The presentation reduces the ROW application to a matter of tribal and individual consent. Our compliance burden is substantially more detailed.

*   **Operationally Inaccurate:** The presentation fails to acknowledge numerous mandatory components of the application, including:
    *   Executing a stipulation that includes all 11 conditions listed in 25 C.F.R. § 169.5 (a)-(k) (workmanlike construction, damage payments, indemnification, restoration, weed control, fire suppression, road repairs, etc.).
    *   Submitting maps of definite location (25 C.F.R. § 169.6) and associated field notes (25 C.F.R. § 169.7).
    *   Providing affidavits from both the survey engineer and the applicant certifying the accuracy of the survey and maps (25 C.F.R. § 169.9).
    *   Specifying the size and type of pipe (welded, screw-joint, etc.).
    *   Making a substantial financial deposit with the Secretary to cover consideration, damages, and severance fees (25 C.F.R. § 169.14).

**4. Inaccurate Framing of Tribal Consultation.**
The presentation mentions consulting with the Tribal Historic Preservation Office and Environmental Office but misrepresents the nature of this interaction.

*   **Operational Inaccuracy:** Document 2 clarifies that after receiving permission to survey, we "should coordinate said survey with the Tribal Historic Preservation Office and the Fort Berthold Agency Environmental Office." This is a procedural directive, not merely a suggestion. Furthermore, these offices must be engaged as part of the overall process, which the presentation frames too vaguely.

**5. Failure to Acknowledge the 20-Year Term Limit.**
The presentation does not mention the regulatory limitations on the duration of the grant.

*   **Legally Incomplete:** Document 2 states that rights-of-way for oil and gas pipelines are limited to a **20-year period** (25 C.F.R. § 169.25 (b)), renewable by application. This is a critical business consideration that the Tribal presentation omits.

**Conclusion and Directive:**

The Tribal presentation, while well-intentioned, presents an idealized and incomplete version of the regulatory process. It should not be used as a guide for our operations. We must continue to follow the exacting procedures outlined in Document 2. I have updated our internal compliance checklist to explicitly counter the inaccuracies in the Tribal presentation. All teams must adhere strictly to the BIA-mandated steps for permission to survey, application for right-of-way, and post-construction requirements.

Do not proceed with any project on the Fort Berthold Reservation without ensuring every single requirement from Document 2 has been met.

Regards,

Legal Compliance Officer
